edges.description: The null and thermolabile alleles together leave too little active KHK-C, the hepatic isoform, at body temperature.
Without ketohexokinase, the liver cannot carry out the first step of fructose catabolism, so no fructose 1-phosphate is formed after a fructose load.
Fructose that escapes hepatic phosphorylation stays in the blood, so blood fructose rises higher and clears more slowly after a load.

nodes.description: Both KHK alleles carry deficient variants. In the index family one allele is effectively null (p.Gly40Arg) and the other encodes a thermolabile enzyme (p.Ala43Thr).

nodes.description: The fructose that is neither metabolized in liver nor excreted is phosphorylated at C6 by hexokinase in skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, entering glycolysis as fructose 6-phosphate. This route is slow, which is consistent with the slow clearance of blood fructose. It is an alternative pathway rather than a disease mechanism, and no clinical consequence of it is known.

nodes.description: Hepatocytes cannot convert fructose to fructose 1-phosphate, so the normal rapid first-pass hepatic uptake and catabolism of dietary fructose does not occur. Because fructose 1-phosphate does not accumulate, hepatic ATP and inorganic phosphate are not depleted after a fructose load, unlike the transient depletion in healthy people and the persistent depletion in hereditary fructose intolerance.

nodes.description: A mathematical model of oral and intravenous fructose disposition, calibrated to healthy subjects and then adapted to reproduce published essential fructosuria data. To fit those data the model needed adaptations beyond hepatic KHK loss: altered portal absorption, slower peripheral metabolism, near-absent renal fructose reabsorption, and upregulated alternative hepatic pathways. These are model predictions, not measurements.
